newsitem.title: JAPAN: Showa Shell blames 1996 profit dip on retail price.
newsitem.headline: Showa Shell blames 1996 profit dip on retail price.

text.p: Showa Shell Sekiyu KK said on Friday that poor retail prices for oil products and strong crude prices combined to send its 1996 profits sharply lower.
"Price-cutting competition among gasoline stations and high crude costs created a very difficult business environment," Ralph Gaskell, vice president of Showa Shell Sekiyu, told reporters.
Earlier in the day, Showa Shell Sekiyu said its current profits in the year to December 31 had fallen by 36.2 percent from the previous year to 12.18 billion yen.
Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities, such as investment in stocks.
In 1996, retail prices of middle distillates such as kerosene and gas oil improved slightly, Showa Shell said.
But retail prices of its mainstay product, gasoline, were weak because of a price war in major cities, Gaskell said.
The entrance of supermarkets into the gasoline retail market in suburban areas also did not help, he said.

While gasoline stations were racing to cut prices, global crude prices climbed steadily. The precipitous fall in the value of the yen against the dollar in late 1996 also helped push the cost of crude up sharply in Japan, Showa Shell said.

In yen-based terms, the price of Dubai crude, a Middle Eastern crude used as a benchmark in Asia, rose 41.4 percent in 1996 because of strong crude prices and the yen's depreciation against the dollar, the company said.
It added that its sales volume of oil products fell by 5.7 percent from the previous year to 47.58 million kilolitres.
Gaskell said the fall could be attributed to stagnant demand for fuel oil C from electric utilities, which increased their use of nuclear power, coal and liquefied natural gas.
For 1997, Showa Shell forecast a current profit of 20.00 billion yen.
"A harsh business environment is expected to continue in 1997. However, it is unlikely that crude prices will rise further or that the yen's depreciation will continue," Gaskell said.
Japanese refiners lost their monopoly on imports of products such as gasoline and kerosene after last year's industry deregulation and are struggling to survive competition from abroad.
Asked whether a merger with Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd was likely to materialise, Gaskell said: "It is too early to give any indications. We are studying every possibility."
He added: "We are still in the stage of an internal study."

Showa Shell said on Monday it was considering merging its oil refining and distribution divisions with those of Mitsubishi Oil Co Ltd, but leaving the retail units separate, as part of an effort to cut costs.
Showa Shell Sekiyu KK is owned 50 percent by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group.
